enrichment.short_title: Limitation on collateral warranty breach for defective VAV units
key_facts: Procter & Gamble claimed damages for defective Carrier 37 HS variable air volume units installed at Brooklands headquarters in 1995.
Claims were based on collateral contractual warranty, negligent misrepresentation, and negligence arising from pre-contract representations to architects Aukett.
Proceedings were issued against Toshiba in October 2000 and amended in February 2001 to add Carrier and a collateral contract claim.
Three preliminary issues asked whether contract, negligent misrepresentation, and negligence causes of action accrued before key limitation dates.
On assumed facts, breach of the collateral warranty occurred on delivery completion on 21 February 1995, and relevant tort loss was not suffered earlier.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary limitation issues and associated applications to substitute Carrier, disallow claim form amendments, and amend particulars to plead collateral contract.
enrichment.outcome: All three preliminary issues answered No; application to disallow 16 February 2001 amendments dismissed; court would have granted substitution and collateral contract amendment applications if necessary.
enrichment.ratio: Breach of a collateral contractual warranty as to product performance accrues when non-compliant goods are delivered, not when the warranty is made; in negligent misrepresentation and negligence claims for defective supplied goods, relevant economic loss is suffered when the claimant acquires property in defective units, not when earlier contracts are entered.
legal_issues: When a cause of action for breach of collateral warranty accrues
When causes of action in negligent misrepresentation and negligence accrue for purely economic loss
Whether amendments adding Carrier and a collateral contract claim were valid under CPR 17.1 and 19.4
Whether substitution of Carrier for Toshiba was permitted under CPR 19.5

enrichment.short_title: Adjudication referral upheld despite premature final account dispute

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Costain, main contractor, applied under Part 8 for a declaration that Wescol Steel's adjudication referral was invalid.
Steelwork was substantially complete around July 2002; Wescol entered administrative receivership in September 2002.
Costain argued no dispute existed over the final account because payment was not yet due and notice/service requirements were defective.
Wescol claimed about £921,000 on variations and sought adjudication on final account value and extension of time.
Referral documents were not sent by fax and first-class post as required by subcontract clause 38A.9.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 application for declaration that a JCT subcontract adjudication referral was invalid.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; adjudication referral held valid.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute over the value of a final account can exist where a claim is made and not admitted or paid, even if the paying party is still examining documents; multiple related claims may constitute one dispute; failure to comply with contractual notice provisions does not invalidate an adjudicator's decision where the contract provides that such failure shall not do so.
legal_issues: When a construction dispute sufficient for adjudication has arisen
Whether one notice may refer multiple related disputes
Effect of non-compliance with contractual service requirements on validity of adjudication
Interaction of clause 38A.9 and clause 38A.5.6 in JCT adjudication provisions

Halki Shipping Corporation v Sopex Oils Ltd

enrichment.short_title: Auditor denied relief over council-funded officers' libel claims
key_facts: Bedford Borough Council agreed to fund and indemnify libel claims by senior officers against a local newspaper and a Conservative election agent.
The dispute followed press criticism of council handling of missed postal votes in the May 2000 Brickhill ward election.
Officers partially succeeded at trial before Gray J but were ordered to pay about 80% of defendants' costs, estimated above £500,000.
The appointed auditor challenged the indemnity as ultra vires nearly two years after the executive committee decision of 7 June 2000.
The auditor conceded undue delay and substantial hardship to the officers if relief were granted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by an Audit Commission-appointed auditor of a local authority decision to fund officers' defamation proceedings and indemnify costs.
enrichment.outcome: Relief refused on grounds of extreme delay under section 31(6); application dismissed, though the court held the council had power under section 111 to grant the indemnity.
enrichment.ratio: An auditor may not obtain late judicial review relief where there was extreme delay and granting relief would cause very substantial hardship, even where a point of legal principle arises; funding an officer's offensive defamation proceedings may fall within section 111 if conducive to employment functions, subject to ordinary public law control and without circumventing Derbyshire's prohibition on authority libel actions.
legal_issues: Whether a local authority may fund offensive defamation proceedings by officers under section 111
Distinction between defensive and offensive litigation indemnities
Whether Derbyshire County Council v Times Newspapers creates a defamation exception to section 111
Effect of delay and hardship under section 31(6) on auditor challenges

enrichment.short_title: Council employee fails stress and bullying liability claim
key_facts: Michael Barlow, a long-serving Broxbourne council operations manager, claimed psychiatric injury from alleged bullying and workplace stress between 1997 and September 1998.
Management changes followed compulsory competitive tendering; Mr Robertson reduced Barlow's duties from March 1996.
Specific incidents included Robertson swearing at Barlow in July and September 1998 over operational failures.
Dr Leadbeater sent numerous disciplinary letters in mid-1998; Barlow broke down on 7 September 1998 and never returned to work.
Medical evidence established a moderate depressive episode, but managers said Barlow appeared phlegmatic and gave no clear warning signals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Split trial on liability only in an employer's liability personal injury claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on liability; neither bullying/victimisation nor stress-related negligence established.
enrichment.ratio: Isolated foul language by a manager exasperated by operational failures does not cumulatively amount to bullying where harm was not reasonably foreseeable; an employer is not in breach of duty for occupational stress unless psychiatric injury to the particular employee was reasonably foreseeable on plain indications, applying the Hatton v Sutherland principles.
legal_issues: Whether conduct amounted to bullying or victimisation
Foreseeability of psychiatric harm in workplace stress claims
Application of Hatton v Sutherland to a local authority employee
Whether a barrage of disciplinary correspondence rendered harm foreseeable

confidence.notes: Liability-only outcome and Hatton-based stress analysis are explicit. EC Directive 89/391 was pleaded but not pursued at trial.

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan asylum appeal restored for wanted returnee risk

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Mr Selvaratnam, a Sri Lankan Tamil, claimed asylum after clandestine arrival in September 2001.
He had been arrested and tortured in 1995-1996 and again from November 2000, then escaped unlawful detention.
The adjudicator accepted his evidence and found a real risk of arrest and torture on return.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal based on improved country conditions for returned asylum seekers.
The IAT did not adequately address the applicant's status as a recently detained, wanted person rather than a generic failed asylum seeker.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision allowing the Secretary of State's appeal from an adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT decision set aside and adjudicator's decision restored.
enrichment.ratio: Where updated country guidance indicates most returned asylum seekers may return safely, a tribunal must still ask whether the individual is an exceptional case; a person recently detained, tortured, and having escaped custody as a wanted individual remains at risk of detention and torture on return, distinct from the general returned-asylum-seeker analysis.
legal_issues: Proper application of updated Sri Lanka country guidance
Whether the applicant was an exceptional case as a wanted returnee
Risk of torture once detained in Sri Lanka
Scope of appellate review of IAT fact-finding
linked_authorities: Jeyachandran

confidence.notes: Outcome and distinguishing reasoning are clear. Judges array is empty in the source metadata though Buxton, May, and Peter Gibson LJJ delivered the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Hello! defence survives despite false Court of Appeal evidence
key_facts: Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones granted OK! exclusive wedding photograph rights; Hello! published unauthorised pictures from Philip Ramey.
Hello! obtained interlocutory injunction discharge in the Court of Appeal partly on evidence later admitted to be false.
False statements included claims that Neneto Overseas Ltd sold UK rights and that Hello! had no prior knowledge of the photographs.
Hello! destroyed or failed to preserve emails, electronic photograph files, and invoices relating to acquisition of the pictures.
The claimants applied to strike out Hello!'s defences and to re-amend to plead conspiracy and exemplary damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Pre-trial applications to strike out defences for abuse of process, to re-amend particulars of claim, and to strike out claims against the Marquesa and NOL.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to re-amend granted; strike-out applications against Hello!, the Marquesa, and NOL dismissed; fair trial still possible.
enrichment.ratio: Knowingly false interlocutory evidence and post-commencement destruction of relevant documents are serious litigation misconduct, but they do not automatically strike out a defence unless they render a fair trial impossible or unsafe; publication of confidential wedding photographs may ground direct publisher liability, and conspiracy by unlawful means may include post-injunction concealment notwithstanding witness immunity limits on individual evidence claims.
legal_issues: Whether false Court of Appeal evidence justified striking out Hello!'s defence
Effect of destroyed documents on fairness of trial
Whether the Marquesa and NOL were joint tortfeasors or direct publishers
Admissibility of conspiracy claims based on false evidence and document destruction
Availability of exemplary damages against private defendants

enrichment.short_title: 1980 murder conviction replaced with diminished responsibility manslaughter
key_facts: Haddon was convicted of murder in 1980 for killing his ten-week-old daughter by swinging her against a hard surface.
At trial he admitted hitting the baby but denied causing the fatal skull fracture; a co-accused was acquitted of murder.
The 1980 prison medical report found emotional immaturity but no psychopathic disorder warranting further investigation.
New psychiatric evidence from Dr Walsh and Dr Clark diagnosed severe personality disorder traceable to childhood deprivation.
The Crown accepted that had this evidence been available at trial a different verdict would likely have resulted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by reference of the Criminal Cases Review Commission against a 1980 murder conviction; sentence adjourned.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; murder conviction quashed and substituted with manslaughter on grounds of diminished responsibility; sentencing adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh psychiatric evidence showing the appellant suffered at the time of the offence from a severe personality disorder constituting an abnormality of mind substantially impairing responsibility, which was not appreciated at trial using outdated diagnostic criteria, can justify substituting a manslaughter verdict long after conviction where the Crown accepts the evidence would have changed the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether new personality disorder evidence established diminished responsibility under section 2 Homicide Act 1957
Whether the disorder existed at the time of the offence rather than developing in prison
Appropriate substituted verdict under section 3 Criminal Appeal Act 1968
Legality of continued hospital remand pending sentence

confidence.notes: Substituted verdict and psychiatric reasoning are clear. Sentence was not determined at this hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Magistrate removal quashed for non-compliant complaints panel
key_facts: Mr Gill, a Newcastle upon Tyne magistrate, was accused of telling a pub licensee he could use his position to get the licence revoked.
An Advisory Committee complaints panel preferred the complainant's evidence and recommended removal from office.
The panel comprised four Newcastle bench magistrates plus one non-magistrate, contrary to Lord Chancellor's Directions paragraph 19.16.
Those directions required at least one magistrate member from a different bench where practicable.
The Lord Chancellor accepted the recommendation and removed Mr Gill in November 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Lord Chancellor's decision removing a magistrate following an Advisory Committee complaints investigation hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; removal decision quashed and matter remitted for rehearing by a properly constituted panel.
enrichment.ratio: A magistrate facing removal is entitled to a fair procedure under the Lord Chancellor's Directions; paragraph 19.16 requires at least one panel magistrate from a different bench, and failure to comply breaches legitimate expectation even where no actual bias is shown, absent good reason for departure.
legal_issues: Whether Lord Chancellor's Directions paragraph 19.16 created a legitimate expectation
Effect of metropolitan single-bench advisory committee areas on panel composition
Whether breach of guidelines vitiated removal despite absence of demonstrated bias
Distinction between mandatory and prescriptive procedural guidance

enrichment.short_title: Noise prosecution stayed because defendant unfit to stand trial
key_facts: Mr Wotton, aged 62 and living in sheltered accommodation, was prosecuted for breaching noise abatement notices after using heavy tools at anti-social hours.
Following a stroke he developed cognitive impairment, disinhibited behaviour, and unreliable memory according to Dr Packer.
By February 2002 Dr Packer concluded Wotton was not fit to stand trial and his condition was likely progressive.
Honiton magistrates refused a stay, relying on legal representation and equality of arms.
Mid Devon District Council did not contest the judicial review or adduce contrary medical evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' refusal to stay criminal proceedings for breach of noise abatement notices.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; prosecution stayed except for possible exercise of equipment retention/disposal powers under the Noise Act 1996 schedule; matter remitted to magistrates.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant adjudged on proper uncontested medical evidence to be unfit to stand trial must not be subjected to criminal proceedings; Article 6 and common law require capacity to understand the charge, participate, and give instructions, which legal representation alone cannot cure.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates erred in refusing to stay proceedings where medical evidence showed unfitness to stand trial
Minimum requirements for a fair criminal trial under Article 6
Availability of equipment disposal powers under the Noise Act 1996 without conviction
Inapplicability of section 11 Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000 where offence not imprisonable
linked_authorities: V v the United Kingdom

confidence.notes: Stay order and Article 6 reasoning are straightforward given uncontested psychiatric evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Homeless duty requires ongoing suitability review of temporary housing
key_facts: Mr Zaher and his family became homeless when their Westminster flat burned down in June 2001.
Westminster accepted a section 193 duty and placed the family in temporary accommodation at Laurel Lane, West Drayton in October 2001 after initial refusal.
In June 2002 the family asked to move citing distance from school, family support, wife's depression, and overcrowding as a fourth child was expected.
Westminster refused transfer, directing the claimant first to seek a move through Eurolet Management Services and treating the accommodation as still suitable.
The council did not conduct a section 202 review of the June 2002 refusal despite solicitor requests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned application for permission to apply for judicial review, treated as substantive hearing, of Westminster's refusal to review housing suitability or transfer temporary accommodation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; decision of 14 June 2002 quashed; Westminster directed to reconsider suitability of the accommodation.
enrichment.ratio: A housing authority's duty under sections 193 and 206 to secure suitable accommodation is continuing during the duty period and is not discharged once and for all on acceptance of short-term temporary housing; where circumstances change materially, the authority must reconsider suitability, and an unwarranted requirement to obtain Eurolet approval before any review is an unlawful fetter on that discretion.
legal_issues: Whether suitability under section 206 is a continuing duty or fixed at initial acceptance
Effect of Alghile v Westminster on later challenges to accepted temporary accommodation
Whether section 175(3) applies when accommodation becomes unsuitable
Whether judicial review was precluded by section 204 County Court appeal route
Whether the June 2002 letter was a reviewable decision
